name: Craig Jones Riding Control System
description: Study Craig Jones riding control with a focused Power Ride course guide, positional practice ideas, and links connecting top control, turtle and back attacks.
summary: The Craig Jones Riding Control System is a BJJGraph study guide for developing top control through connected rides and pins, with Power Ride as its instructional companion.
overview:
Craig Jones teaches a riding approach in Power Ride: A New Philosophy on Pinning. Its published syllabus connects lower-body control, upper-body tools, turtle work and submission entries. It is a specific fit for the problem of passing guard and then losing the opponent during their next movement.

The sequence below is BJJGraph's suggested practice plan, not a transcript of the course or an official Craig Jones curriculum. Choose a familiar position, investigate where control is lost, and test one adjustment with a partner. Learning to retain top position can be useful even when no submission appears. A coach can help select controls appropriate to the pair and connect the material to their existing game.
key_principles: Give each practice round a concrete control objective that both partners understand.
Notice which connection is lost before adding another grip or changing position.
Treat a recovered guard or successful stand-up as feedback about the preceding transition.
Keep a stable base while testing a new control; more pressure cannot replace balance.
Add submission entries only after partners can practise the underlying position reliably.
Distinguish holding someone down from meeting the scoring requirements of a particular match.

key_components.description: Choose one familiar top position and record how the bottom partner usually begins to escape.
key_components.purpose: Create a repeatable problem instead of testing every possible ride at once.

key_components.description: Identify the contact that prevents a comfortable turn and the contact that can be released without immediately losing balance.
key_components.purpose: Explain a control in terms that can be checked during slow practice.

key_components.description: Let the bottom partner change direction within an agreed range while the top partner attempts to remain connected.
key_components.purpose: Develop recognition of changing movement without prescribing a fixed sequence.

key_components.description: When the original pin fails, choose between a familiar adjacent position and a clean reset.
key_components.purpose: Avoid interpreting every lost grip as a reason to chase a submission.

key_components.description: Check that a chosen submission entry does not immediately surrender the position established in the previous phase.
key_components.purpose: Evaluate the tradeoff between control and an attacking opportunity.

implementation_sequence.description: Begin from side control or another position both partners already understand. Agree the bottom partner's escape goal and a reset condition.
Use a cooperative round to identify when the bottom partner first gains room to turn or recover guard. Stop and name that moment.
Select one relevant lesson with a coach. Practise the adjustment slowly and confirm both partners understand its purpose.
Allow a different escape direction. Check whether the adjustment transfers or whether another familiar position is a better choice.
Introduce one agreed submission entry only after the control task is repeatable. Release immediately on any tap or request to stop.
Write down whether the attempted attack improved the situation, preserved control, or allowed an escape. Choose the next round from that result.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The drill turns into an unrestricted scramble.
common_obstacles.solution: Narrow the starting position and reset when either partner reaches the agreed endpoint.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The top player squeezes harder as balance deteriorates.
common_obstacles.solution: Pause before the turnover and identify where base was lost; return to cooperative practice.

common_obstacles.obstacle: A successful attack hides repeated positional losses.
common_obstacles.solution: Record control losses separately from taps so the drill still measures the intended skill.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The bottom player gives the same reaction every repetition.
common_obstacles.solution: Introduce another agreed direction only after the first response is comfortable.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The practitioner treats a study guide as full technical instruction.
common_obstacles.solution: Use the linked course or a coach for detailed demonstrations and use this page to organise practice.

assessment_metrics.description: Can the practitioner identify the first meaningful loss of control?
proficiency_indicators: Locates the moment before the escape completes
Chooses a relevant adjustment to test

assessment_metrics.description: Assess whether changing grips or direction preserves a workable top position.
proficiency_indicators: Recognises when the original pin is gone
Can select a familiar recovery position

assessment_metrics.description: Record which agreed escape directions have been tested.
proficiency_indicators: Adjusts the drill when a new reaction appears
Can explain the limits of the current solution

assessment_metrics.description: Review whether an attack was supported by the position.
proficiency_indicators: Can delay an attack when control is weak
Can stop safely on any partner signal
Records escapes caused by premature attacks

training_methodology.drilling_approach: These are BJJGraph practice suggestions rather than course assignments. Start with cooperative movement from one familiar pin. Give the bottom partner a clear escape objective and keep the top player focused on control. Increase resistance only when both partners can stop comfortably and explain what changed. Ask a coach to review uncertain controls before adding submission attempts.

progression_path.focus: Describe one recurring escape and the contact lost before it.
Practise one selected control with cooperative movement.
Test another escape direction under the same starting conditions.
Add one agreed attack and track whether top control survives.

common_mistakes: Changing several controls at once and losing track of what helped.
Using a tap count as the only measure of a control drill.
Continuing through discomfort instead of resetting and asking for feedback.

flashcards.question: What does this guide ask you to measure before counting submissions?
flashcards.answer: Measure whether top control survives the partner's agreed escape attempt and identify the first connection lost when it fails.

flashcards.question: Why should a riding-control drill begin from one familiar position?
flashcards.answer: A repeatable starting point makes it easier to compare reactions and see whether a selected adjustment actually improves control.

flashcards.question: What should happen when the drill becomes an uncontrolled scramble?
flashcards.answer: Reset to the agreed starting position and narrow the available reactions so both partners can recognise the problem being tested.

flashcards.question: How can an unsuccessful round still provide useful information?
flashcards.answer: Identify the moment control was lost, then use that observation to choose a smaller problem for the next round.

flashcards.question: When should a submission entry be added to the control task?
flashcards.answer: Add an agreed entry when both partners can practise the underlying control reliably and can stop immediately on any partner signal.

flashcards.question: Are the practice stages on this page official Power Ride assignments?
flashcards.answer: No. They are BJJGraph study suggestions; use the instructional demonstrations and coaching for detailed technical instruction.

products.title: Power Ride: A New Philosophy on Pinning
products.blurb: Connects leg rides, upper-body controls and turtle breakdowns to submission opportunities.
products.best_for: No-gi players who pass guard but struggle to keep a mobile opponent down; this is a control course, not a complete passing curriculum.
products.study_focus: Begin with the movement principles, then compare one leg-control lesson with an upper-body tool.
products.practice_tip: BJJGraph suggestion: start in an agreed top position and score a controlled recovery after your partner changes direction. Use no submissions initially.
